That is the whole workflow. Everything below is detail.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Load the commands first

Paste this once each time you open RStudio. It is one line, and it never
changes:

```r
source("https://gph-2182.github.io/gph2182.R")
```

Inside an exercise project it loads by itself, so you will rarely need to type
it after the first exercise.
:::

## Once per computer: `gph_setup()`

```r
gph_setup()
```

It installs anything missing, asks for your name and email, and walks you
through creating and storing a GitHub token. Run it again any time to confirm
things are still connected; it is safe to repeat.

If you would rather understand each piece, the long version is in
[Connecting RStudio to GitHub](guides/github-setup.qmd).

## Once per exercise: accept, then `gph_start(N)`

1. **Accept the assignment.** The link is on that week's page, for example
   [Weekly Exercise 2](weeks/week-02.qmd). This creates a private GitHub
   repository that belongs to you. Do it once per exercise.
2. **Open it in RStudio.** In the Console:

   ```r
   gph_start(2)
   ```

   Use the exercise number you are working on. That is the whole step: no URL
   to copy, no dialog to fill in, no folder to choose. It works out which
   repository is yours, downloads it into `~/gph2182`, and opens it as a
   project.

If you have not accepted yet, `gph_start()` says so and prints the link you
need. If you already have the exercise on your computer, it just opens it.

## Then repeat: edit, check, submit

### Edit

Open `exercise.qmd`. Put your name in the `author:` field. Answer each question
by replacing `NULL` with your code.

Keep the object names exactly as given (`q1`, `q2`, and so on). The checks look
for those names, so renaming them loses points even when your code is right.

### Check

```r
gph_check()
```

This runs **the same checks GitHub will run**, on your machine, in about two
seconds. You get a PASS or FAIL line per question. Fix the FAIL lines and run
it again. Nothing is submitted and nobody sees the result.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
`gph_check()` runs in a separate, clean R session on purpose. That means it
cannot be fooled by an answer that only exists in your Environment pane rather
than in the file, which is the most common reason work passes locally and fails
on GitHub.
:::

### Submit

```r
gph_submit()
```

One command does all of it: stages your files, commits them, pushes to GitHub,
then waits for GitHub's own check and tells you the result in the Console. You
do not have to visit the Actions tab, though `gph_actions()` opens it if you
want to look.

## What the results mean

| What you see | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `Everything passes` from `gph_check()` | Your file is right on your machine | `gph_submit()` |
| `Pushed to GitHub` | Your work is submitted and safe | Wait for the check result |
| `everything passes. You are done.` | GitHub agrees. Finished | Nothing |
| `something still fails` | Your push arrived but a question is wrong | `gph_check()`, fix, `gph_submit()` |
| `No result yet` | GitHub is busy | Wait a minute, or run `gph_actions()` |

**Submitting many times is normal and expected.** Only your last push before
the deadline is graded, so a failing check on an early attempt costs you
nothing. Push early and often: work on GitHub cannot be lost.

## When something goes wrong

```r
gph_doctor()
```

It prints a ✓ or ✗ for every single thing that has to be true, in order:
packages, your Git name and email, your token, whether this folder is really a
repository, whether anything is uncommitted, whether anything is unpushed, and
what GitHub said about your last submission. The first ✗ is your problem, and
each line tells you which command fixes it.

If you are still stuck, look the exact error message up on the
[error messages page](guides/troubleshooting.qmd), then send me or Sabrina the
output of `gph_doctor()`. That output contains no secrets and usually makes the
answer obvious in one reply.

## Doing it by hand

The commands above are a convenience, not a hiding place. Git and GitHub are
part of what this course teaches, and you should be able to do this without the
helpers by the end of the semester.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## The same five steps, done manually

1. **Clone:** copy your repository URL from GitHub, then in RStudio
   **File > New Project > Version Control > Git**, paste the URL, choose your
   `~/gph2182` folder, and click **Create Project**.
2. **Edit:** open `exercise.qmd` and answer the questions.
3. **Stage:** in the **Git** tab, tick the box next to each changed file.
4. **Commit:** click **Commit**, read the diff, write a message, click
   **Commit**.
5. **Push:** click the green **Push** arrow. Then open your repository on
   github.com and click the **Actions** tab to see the result.

Each of these is explained in full in
[RStudio projects and cloning a repository](guides/rstudio-projects.qmd) and
[Committing, pushing, and pulling](guides/commit-push.qmd).
:::

## Every command, in one place

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `gph_setup()` | Connect RStudio to GitHub. Once per computer |
| `gph_start(N)` | Download and open exercise `N`. Once per exercise |
| `gph_check()` | Run the autograder's checks locally |
| `gph_submit()` | Stage, commit, push, and report the result |
| `gph_actions()` | Open this exercise's Actions page in a browser |
| `gph_doctor()` | Check everything and say what is wrong |
| `gph_help()` | Print the loop again |
